fullText:
While legacy automakers tap the brakes on electric vehicles, one startup is hitting the accelerator. Earlier this month, electric truck maker Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D round, capping a banner stretch that includes a $300 million order from FedEx and a new defense contract with the US military.

Harbinger is stacking up wins by skipping the consumer EV hype cycle altogether and focusing on the unglamorous workhorses that keep the economy running: Class 4–6 delivery vans and box trucks. The company’s thesis is simple: go after the overlooked commercial segments where legacy trucks are weak and giant automakers can’t be bothered to compete, CEO John Harris tells me.

“We’re not solving the big obvious problem because everyone’s going to solve that problem, and as a result, the margins get kind of ground down to zero,” Harris says. “We’re solving problems that — they’ve just been there forever and you no longer think of this as a problem, you just think of it as like part of existence. It’s like a tax on your life.”

Founded in 2021 by veterans of Canoo, QuantumScape, and Faraday Future, Harbinger aims to fill a structural gap in the auto market, in which most passenger EV platforms lack the durability to scale up while the heavy-duty platforms are too heavy and expensive to scale down.

“In auto, you have Class 1 companies and you have Class 8 companies,” Harris says. “And everything in between is kind of a wasteland... It is much, much, much too small for a big company to serve.”

Which is not to say the industry hasn’t tried. Ford and GM both took shots at electrifying the medium-duty segment with the E-Transit and BrightDrop delivery vans, respectively, but sluggish sales and the loss of federal incentives forced them to discontinue or cancel those models.

Harris says that big automakers are ill-suited to task, with their over-reliance on third-party suppliers to build all the necessary components. The effort becomes too spread out and expensive, with not enough return on your investment. That’s why Harbinger is attempting a more vertically integrated approach, he says, assembling its own battery packs and drive units in house — with inverters to follow.

“If you are not vertically integrated in auto, you don’t build viable products,” Harris says. “We believe that electric vehicles are only viable when they’re competitive on acquisition price with combustion vehicles.”

Of course, Harris and his fellow cofounders have tasted failure in their previous ventures. Harbinger’s CTO Phillip Weicker cofounded EV startup Canoo, which ran out of cash and filed bankruptcy in 2025. Harris himself spent a year at tumultuous Chinese EV company Faraday Future before moving on to Xos Trucks and then Palmer Luckey’s Anduril.

“I was an engineer at Faraday. I wasn’t in charge of anything,” Harris says. “So it’s not like, ‘John, why did Faraday not succeed?’ I can tell you lots of reasons, but it wasn’t because the plastic part that I designed didn’t work. It was because the plastic part that I designed was going into a vehicle for which the world customer base was like three people.”

Those companies “fundamentally didn’t work,” he adds, “because of the market fit issue and the leadership issue. Not because the engineering didn’t work or electrification wasn’t ready or they didn’t have enough capital.”

Harbinger’s approach is more pragmatic, offering both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains for its medium-duty trucks. The company is not pursuing heavy-duty Class 8 trucks like the Tesla Semi, however, as Harris argues the economics of electric long-haul trucking are unworkable.

“Class 8 electrification to me is one of those markets. I completely reject the notion that that’s a good fit for electrification for the majority of the market,” he says. “We can put [the Tesla Semi] on the watch list with the Cybertruck.”

With companies like Amazon and FedEx making serious moves to secure more electric delivery vehicles, Harbinger is well-positioned to be a key supplier. And with diesel prices skyrocketing as a result of the war with Iran, more companies are waking up to a reality in which EVs can help bring down their costs.

Harbinger isn’t just building delivery trucks — it’s also branching into energy storage and military technology. For example, the company supplies battery power systems to Airstream and partners with American Rheinmetall and Forterra to build self-driving hybrid supply vehicles for the US Army. Harbinger also recently bought Phantom AI to bring advanced driver-assistance features to commercial fleets, in the hopes of giving companies a clear, measurable return on their safety investments.

With millions in fresh capital and major contracts already on the books, Harbinger has cleared the first major hurdle that tripped up its founders’ past ventures. Now comes the hardest part in the auto business: proving it can actually build them at scale.

“Auto is a big enough opportunity that it can get people’s attention,” Harris says. “It’s also punishingly difficult. So if you can make something that works in auto, it will be phenomenal in every other segment, because every other segment, the competition is essentially weaker.”

title: Google Health 5.13 rolling out: Improved food search, more swimming controls
snippet: Version 5.13 of Google Health is rolling out to Android and iOS with updates across five areas. It’s a modest release that reiterates recent launches. more…
fullText:
Version 5.13 of Google Health is rolling out to Android and iOS with updates across five areas. It’s a modest release that reiterates recent launches.

Google is highlighting the availability of step-by-step workouts on the Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 as part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop. It rolled out with an update to the on-watch Google Health app, while we wait for Wear OS 7.1 to bring the other additions.

There’s also a reminder that apps and clocks are going away on older Fitbit OS smartwatches.

Activity and Fitness Updates

	

In-Progress Automatic Activity Detection: If you use your Pixel Watch, Fitbit Air, or Fitbit Edge to automatically track your exercises, you’ll now see an exercise-in-progress card on your mobile app’s Today screen. This card lets you know that your device is tracking your exercise and gives you the opportunity to end the tracking and get your summary whenever you want.

More Controls for Swimmers: You can now set your default pool length and unit preferences (meters or yards) for your swims for improved distance tracking. Go to your profile, then Google Health settings, and then Activity preferences to change your settings.

Step by Step Workouts: If you use Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5, you can now get live step-by-step guidance on your watch during each exercise in your workout.  Learn more.

Nutrition Updates

Food search has been improved to help you more easily locate items.

More Options for Settings

You can now select ‘Prefer not to say’ or ‘An option not listed’ when selecting your sex during Google Health onboarding. If you select one of these options, you’ll then be asked to choose whether you’d like your metrics to be calculated based on studies of cisgender men or studies of cisgender women.

If your preferences change, you can find these settings at any time in the Health tab by scrolling to Personal info, tapping Profile, and editing your Sex settings.

Apple Health Sync Updates

We’ve fixed an issue that affected a small number of users after the daylight saving time change where Google Health stopped sending some data to Apple Health. Syncing will resume after this fix.  If you were impacted and still have gaps in your Apple Health data, sign out of the Google Health app and sign back in to send any missing data to Apple Health.

Apps and Clocks on Fitbit Smartwatches

Starting on November 28, 2026, you can no longer install or update third-party apps and clocks on Fitbit smartwatches.

After this date, your installed apps and clock faces from third-party developers will continue to work. However, if you choose to delete an app or clock face, or factory reset your device, you will no longer be able to re-install it.

You will continue to have access to a diverse gallery of apps and clocks developed by Fitbit and Google.

This change impacts users of Fitbit Sense, Fitbit Sense 2, Fitbit Versa 4, Fitbit Versa 3, Fitbit Versa 2, Fitbit Versa Lite, and Fitbit Versa.

title: iPadOS 27.3: Three new features coming to your iPad
snippet: iPadOS 27.3 is now in beta and will launch to all users next month, here are three new features it introduces for iPad. more…
fullText:
iPadOS 27.3 is now in beta and will launch to all users next month, here are three new features it introduces for iPad.

#1: Double-tap top of window to resize

There’s a new setting in iPadOS 27.3 that I instantly turned on and have been loving. It lets you double-tap the top of a window to resize it.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if ‘Windowed Apps’ is enabled there’s now a new toggle: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom.’

I’ve been using this gesture all the time in the beta, because it lets me resize my window to fullscreen then revert it to its previous size with ease. It’s an intuitive, convenient way to resize windows for different tasks.

Read more: iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

#2: Siri mode in Camera app

Visual intelligence was available on iPad already, but iPadOS 27.3 adds a dedicated hub for using the feature: a new Siri mode in the Camera app.

iOS 27 brought Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app, but it was missing from iPad. iPadOS 27.3 corrects that oversight, letting you use your iPad’s built-in Camera app to ask Siri about any object you capture.

Baking visual intelligence into Camera should expose the feature to a lot more iPad users, since before you had to set up a custom control or shortcut for it. And with how much better visual intelligence has gotten thanks to Siri AI, the Siri mode is a valuable addition.

Read more: iOS 27 gives the Camera app on iPhone a brand new mode

#3: Freeform gains new powers

Freeform is gaining a variety of new features in iPadOS 27.3. They’re available in macOS and iOS too, but out of all Apple platforms, Freeform feels very much built for the iPad.

New features include:

you can edit images directly in Pixelmator Pro and see the edited version on your board

custom editable shapes can be generated via text descriptions

new text styling options

preset background colors for boards

You’ll need to be an Apple Creator Studio subscriber to get the first two features. On that note, the Creator Studio apps just rolled out a bunch of upgrades this week that you can read about here.

title: iOS 27.3 beta can cause HomeView issues, Apple confirms
snippet: Apple’s new HomeView just launched last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new HomeView just launched last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

HomeView 27.2.1 has Siri AI fixes, but iOS 27.3 beta users are now temporarily unable to perform Personal Content requests

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the company’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail

It’s unknown how many reports of Siri issues on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta users. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

With HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a new issue you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now says: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.

HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.

On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496

— pdfu (@itspdfu) November 19, 2026

It’s understandable that issues might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, users might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

title: Samsung supplier leak suggests mystery ‘bezel-less’ Galaxy S27 display
snippet: There are rumors of a Samsung phone with an “extremely bezel-less” display coming from one of the company’s suppliers, and it might be on one of the next Galaxy S27 models. more…
fullText:
There are rumors of a Samsung phone with an “extremely bezel-less” display coming from one of the company’s suppliers, and it might be on one of the next Galaxy S27 models.

The information comes from a related supplier for Samsung and was brought up by a known leaker, Lanzuk. Their Naver post specifically mentions an “extremely bezel-less” display. What that means is up for debate, and machine translation does not clarify the original post in Korean.

The big takeaway might be that Samsung is looking to launch one of these bezel-less display options within the Galaxy S27 lineup. An early adoption might indicate that even though this supplier planned on developing these displays for an upcoming Galaxy device, Samsung may want to push the timeline forward and fit it to one of the Galaxy S27 series phones.

Which device would debut a new “extremely bezel-less” display is up in the air. Odds are it would be the most expensive option’s display that gets updated – the Galaxy S27 Ultra. It’s also possible it could show up on both the Pro and Ultra variants, to stretch the premium tag across the upper end of the lineup.

	

This leak is probably best taken with a grain of salt. The author seems to have doubts, and this seems like a 50/50 shot. But even if Samsung doesn’t shave the bezels off of one of the Galaxy S27 models, this leak still indicates a future device will get a similar display.

That previously planned iteration may even be a better version than anything the Galaxy S27 series could have. More than a proof-of-concept.

The Galaxy S27 series is expected to launch early next year. In the meantime, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is nearly bezel-less, folds, and is marked down at its best price for the holidays.

title: Siri Modular Apple Watch face gains two new styles with watchOS 27.3
snippet: Siri Modular, the new Apple Watch face in watchOS 27, is gaining new style options. watchOS 27.3, currently in beta, adds two more style options to the existing set. This gives users five options for adjusting what type of information appears on Siri Modular. more…
fullText:
Siri Modular, the new Apple Watch face in watchOS 27, is gaining new style options. watchOS 27.3, currently in beta, adds two more style options to the existing set. This gives users five options for adjusting what type of information appears on Siri Modular. 

watchOS 27.3 adds two Siri-focused styles to Siri Modular

Siri Modular originally shipped with three style options. Each supports a small line complication above the time. 

Additionally, the original three styles include these options:

Large digital click + three circular complications

Compact digital clock + Smart Stack tile + three circular complications 

Large digital clock + Smart Stack tile

In watchOS 27.3, Apple introduces two new Siri features that work with Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

First, there’s Siri Recap which uses the Apple Watch to turn audio into high-level text summaries. Second, there’s Live Rewind which lets you view a transcript of the last 15 seconds of spoken word.

The two new Siri Modular Apple Watch face styles help surface three things: invoking Siri, viewing conversations with Siri, and viewing Siri Recaps on the Apple Watch.

The new styles include a pill-shaped module that includes icon shortcuts that go directly to Siri conversations, invoke Siri AI, or go directly to Siri Recaps in the Siri app.

One style features a large digital clock with the new three-button Siri module. Another includes a compact digital clock with a Smart Stack tile and the new three-button Siri module.

This brings the style options to five. If you use the three circular complications configuration, you can also assign a Siri icon that invokes Siri AI. 

watchOS 27.3 is currently in beta and expected to be released officially in December.

title: iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3
snippet: iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

#1: Face unlock

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple: 

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

#2: Reachability

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

#3: Automatically lock when closed

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

Bonus: Keyboard updates

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

title: Uber Is Testing Rides for Kids With Qualified Drivers
snippet: The company is testing a ride option for children ages 10 to 12 in select cities for a limited time.
fullText:
Uber, the popular ridesharing app, is testing rides for kids. Uber Kids will cater to youngsters ages 10 to 12, those awkward years before adolescence. The new program expands on the company’s other offering to underage passengers, Uber Teens, which launched in 2023 and provides rides to teenagers ages 13 to 17 in select cities.

The pilot program for Uber Kids starts in three US cities for a limited time: Austin, Texas; Nashville, Tennessee; and Madison, Wisconsin. Its expansion will depend on how well it performs in those regions. If successful, Uber Kids could bring a whole new influx of customers to the app, specifically parents and families needing help getting their kids from point A to point B.

On the surface, it feels like a questionable proposition, given all the potential harms and dangers to young people traveling alone with a stranger. But it seems like Uber took those concerns into account. The rideshare app has added a slew of mandatory requirements for both approved guardians and qualified drivers.

			

More from CNET

First off, kids won’t simply be able to order a ride for themselves. The adult user must add the child to their family profile and complete an onboarding session covering the service’s safety features. They’ll also need to set up PIN verification for every trip. The parent or guardian must be present at the pickup location and provide the driver with a note containing the drop-off instructions.

As any parent would likely wonder (myself included), what about the drivers? How are they vetted?

According to Uber, only the highest-rated drivers will be invited to take part in the program. They’ll need to pass thorough background checks and successfully complete an Uber Kids education curriculum. Moreover, they must agree to use live video streaming in their cars so that parents and guardians can watch the trip every step of the way.

Live videos of underage passengers bring up a bunch of potential red flags, but Uber states all recordings will be encrypted, and no driver will have access to the content. Furthermore, sensors and GPS data will track the ride if the trip is interrupted or veers off course.

Uber could face a tough time recruiting drivers for Uber Kids. Transporting minors adds extra responsibility and requires specific skills that many drivers may want to avoid. To sweeten the deal, Uber is offering eligible drivers a $20 bonus on their first ride and an extra $7 per trip after that.

An Uber spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to our request for comment.

title: iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2 get new release timing updates
snippet: Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing. more…
fullText:
Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing.

iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 suppliers planning for March launch, per report

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh update on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the new models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production plans signal a March release for the products.

Kim Yeong-ho, writing at ETNews:

Samsung Display plans to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside new Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

With Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the new models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

title: Meta Is Trying to Woo Teens to Instagram Through Schools
snippet: Project Gryffindor is an initiative intended to make Instagram popular by marketing “school communities” on the platform.
fullText:
Meta has justifiably attracted more scrutiny than ever this year, along with multibillion-dollar judgments and settlements, over how its business practices affect young social media users. The company, however, is not retreating.

In fact, the tech giant has made a major push toward drawing teenagers to one of its flagship platforms, Instagram, by targeting them at their schools.

According to documents obtained and reported by NPR, Meta launched an initiative called Project Gryffindor, named after a Hogwarts house in the Harry Potter series, to create school communities on Instagram in order to boost user counts and engagement on the platform.

			

More from CNET

Meta’s goal of approaching young users where they spend the most time offline was not a secret. As recently as late September, the company said it was expanding its School Partnership Program, which includes 17,000 schools, with a stated goal to “help students and parents stay informed.”

The company’s internal documents reveal some of the motivations behind Meta’s push for school adoption and Project Gryffindor’s proposed features, such as school banners on teen profiles and the ability to search school directories by class year. The details were acquired as part of discovery in a multistate lawsuit over whether social media platforms are designed to be addictive to users under 18. Meta is a defendant in the case, along with other companies, including TikTok, Snap and Google. 

In 2024, Instagram introduced Teen accounts and has since been trying to assure parents they’re safe while rolling out additional protections. Studies, however, have suggested that young teens regularly encounter unsafe content or deal with unwanted contact. Recruiting more users at an early age without resolving these risks could make teens more vulnerable to mental health issues and increase the chances of being bullied or harassed.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Meta’s business motivations

To anyone familiar with Meta’s long history of privacy oversteps on platforms like Facebook, the documents aren’t surprising. They reveal a company primed to give school-age children new ways to chat and connect with each other, and to encourage them to bring their friends along, expanding Instagram’s user base and engagement. 

Like other social platforms, Instagram primarily makes its money from targeted advertising. User retention is a key part of Meta’s strategy. 

In one of the document slides, titled “Why schools, why now?” which preceded Gryffindor’s launch, Meta said, “Competitors are exploring school social use cases, but IG may be better positioned for school connections thanks to our differentiator of meeting new people and building relationships with acquaintances.” In other words, Instagram’s size and scale, with about 3 billion active users globally, automatically make it a draw for students.

The NPR report comes within a week of a filing against Meta alleging that it’s withholding evidence in a major case involving social media’s effects on teenagers. 

‘Not safe as advertised’

One of Meta’s marketing pitches for its School Partnership Program is that it’s trying to create online safe spaces for students, while giving parents and schools more oversight on what’s accessible on the platform. But experts warn that Meta’s history makes it hard to trust the company with protecting kids from predators or scammers.

Katie Paul, director of the Center for Accountability’s Tech Transparency Project, which has been researching how Meta handles child-safety issues, said that Instagram Teen accounts “are not safe as advertised” and that nothing is “legally requiring the company to make these safe.” Paul pointed out that Instagram launched these accounts only when lawsuits over social media harm started rolling in. 

“It’s all part of a broader marketing (effort) to claim that these are just safer for kids because they are Teen accounts,” Paul said. That marketing effort has included paid endorsements from therapists, psychologists and parent influencers to promote Teen accounts. The case for building up partnerships with schools is a way of “passing the buck on responsibility” to schools and parents, Paul said.

Parents, in particular, have less power in Instagram’s school groups: Unlike the school administrators tasked with managing school groups, parents have no powers to moderate or manage those groups; they can only view them. For Teen accounts in general, parents can’t view direct messages sent to or received by their children.

Meta’s business interests in its push for student engagement and school partnerships are easy to see through. Because kids are likely to be lifetime users on these platforms, getting them hooked early has long-term financial value. 

 “Ultimately, Meta is the one profiting off of the data collection of these kids while simultaneously failing to keep them safe,” Paul said. 

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Omar Gallaga
						

						

											

								

											Omar Gallaga has covered technology, digital culture and other topics for outlets including CNET, NPR, Wired, Texas Monthly, MSNBC, Consumer Reports, The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, The Atlantic and the Austin American-Statesman, where he was a longtime tech reporter, editor and podcaster. He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: The Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess adds new color grading sets, expands to iPhone
snippet: VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone. more…
fullText:
VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with. 

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

	

VWFNDR explains:

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:

B+W
NIHON
NATURAL

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

title: OLED iMac plans may be cancelled by Apple for two reasons
snippet: Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a new supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro. The company is said to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited … more…
fullText:
Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a new supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro.

The company is said to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited …

	

Apple’s journey into OLED screens began with the Apple Watch while other products were still using IPS LCD. The company subsequently switched to OLED for some iPhones and iPads before a long-awaited launch of the first OLED MacBook Pro back in October.

It was expected that the company would gradually transition to OLED across the full range of Macs over time. However, this process was expected to take a number of years, with the iMac not likely to join the party until 2029 or 2030.

OLED iMac may be delayed or abandoned

The Elec today reports that the move may be delayed even further or even abandoned altogether, for two reasons: cost and demand.

The company is said to be discussing a potential delay or cancellation of the project with Samsung Display. High OLED panel costs and weak sales of existing OLED-equipped products are believed to be factors behind the reconsideration […]

The biggest factor behind the review is cost. The iMac sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops, making it difficult to maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted. Weak sales of the OLED iPad Pro are also believed to have influenced the decision. 

The report suggests that incoming CEO John Ternus has been reviewing the commercial viability of upgrading more products to OLED. As further evidence, the report says Apple has sent quotation requests to LCD suppliers for an iMac screen to be launched in around 2029.

title: Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro
snippet: The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead? more…
fullText:
The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?

Over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company. The first time I used a Vivo X100 Pro blew my mind in a way smartphone cameras hadn’t for a few years, but does the company’s 4th iteration — yes, Vivo skipped the X400 — of the X series still impress?

The answer is mostly yes. The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max. Unlike some other phones, all three of these models feature different camera hardware that takes advantage of the physical size differences. The X500 Pro Max’s hardware is the best of the bunch, but that phone is substantially larger and heavier as a result.

So I’m comparing the more reasonably sized models to see which semi-compact Vivo phone you should consider this year. I tossed the Google Pixel 11 Pro into the comparison since Google also offers a compact flagship camera phone.

	

Vivo X500

Vivo X500 Pro

Google Pixel 11 Pro

Main camera

50MP, 1/1.28-inch, f/1.7, 1.22-micron

50MP, 1/1.28-inch, f/1.6, 1.22-micron

50MP, 1/1.3-inch, f/1.7, 1.2-micron

Telephoto camera

64MP, 1/2.0-inch, f/2.6, 0.7-micron, 3x lens

64MP, 1/2.0-inch, f/2.5, 0.7-micron, 3x lens

48MP, 1/1.95-inch, f/2.8, 0.8-micron, 5x lens

Ultrawide camera

50MP, 1/2.76-inch, f/2.0, 0.64-micron, 119-degree lens

50MP, 1/2.75-inch, f/2.0, 0.64-micron, 119-degree lens

48MP, 1/2.51-inch, f/1.7, 0.7-micron, 123-degree lens

Front-facing camera

50MP, 1/2.76-inch, f/2.0, 0.64-micron

50MP, 1/2.76-inch, f/2.0, 0.64-micron

42MP, f/2.2, 0.7-micron

Most camera specs between these phones are surprisingly comparable, so the differences you’re about to see are largely caused by some pretty massive differences in processing. I already covered Vivo’s wild new AI camera mode, so let’s go for something a little closer to normal smartphone camera use: a day at the Biltmore.

Perhaps the biggest difference between these phones is Vivo’s pursuit of “perfection,” while Google seems to embrace a more “natural” look. At 10x and 5x, the photos from both Vivo phones are essentially noise-free, have clear sharpening applied to them, and are generally quite vibrant. Despite having similar specs, the Vivo X500 Pro’s more advanced Sony LYT telephoto sensor pulls out more detail.

Google’s images are notably softer, although not in a low-resolution sort of way. They look more like they’re taken from a standard camera rather than a smartphone, which some people may prefer. While telephoto image quality between the Vivo X500 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro is mostly down to preference, Google’s phone is substantially faster while taking the actual photo. In all of the darker shots, the Pixel 11 Pro took the picture instantly. Both Vivo X500 models took a 2-3 second exposure shot, making me stand there for longer than I’m used to.

Ultrawide performance is where I feel we see the largest gap between these phones. Both the Vivo X500 and X500 Pro cameras offer bright, well-balanced shots that are vibrant but not unrealistic. The light sources in the room emit a lovely warm glow, yet the bulbs themselves aren’t overblown. The X500 Pro’s slightly warmer image across all three scenarios looks best to me.

The Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide images are often underexposed and lacking in dynamic range. The staircase shot exhibits this problem the most. This can come off as natural in some scenarios, as modern smartphone photography is notorious for brightening dark areas too much, but too often the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide shots just feel unnaturally dark.

The main camera is much more balanced, although it’s fun to push these phones to find their weaknesses. One of the best examples of differing priorities is in the wreath shot, which was quite dark in real life thanks to the bright sunlight outside. The Pixel 11 Pro valiantly tried to brighten up the shadows so you could actually see the wreath (since it’s clearly the subject), causing the rest of the scene to look forcefully bright.

The same issue cropped up in the image of the wine rack, where both Vivo phones captured a nicer-looking shot. The image of the trellis walkway is a tie, but the photo of my ridiculous bowl of ice cream looks best on the Vivo X500 Pro, once again.

Portrait mode is where I think the Vivo X500 Pro is the clear loser, but it’s not for any of the reasons in the other categories above. Rather, the X500 Pro seems to have some weird warping happening in the bokeh processing that’s not present on the base Vivo X500. This is in both front-facing and rear camera portrait shots, so it’s not a lens issue or some weird setting.

Google cleaned up its portrait shots so much this year that it’s borderline ridiculous. Pixels had the worst portrait mode for years, but this year’s overhaul of the portrait algorithm made all the difference in the world.

Overall, the Vivo X500 series is another solid release for Vivo, and while neither the base nor Pro models offer the same top-tier camera specs as the Pro Max model, it’s clear Vivo pulled off something great. The Vivo X500 Pro retails for €1,399 in the EU, while the base X500 global model is a little harder to find, but should be quite a bit cheaper if you can get your hands on it.

title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
snippet: "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," California AG Rob Bonta said.
fullText:
California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added.

The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.

The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.

The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors. 

Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote. 

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

fullText:
Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Jensen Huang responds to calls for him to return as CEO, says he would ‘be honored to answer these calls’

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

Here’s what Huang said:

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

	

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

title: One UI 9.5 Beta is out now for these Galaxy devices – how to install it
snippet: Samsung’s beta train has officially left the station, so to speak. One UI 9.5 is starting to roll out to these devices, and with it, some major changes to its Galaxy phones. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s beta train has officially left the station, so to speak. One UI 9.5 is starting to roll out to these devices, and with it, some major changes to its Galaxy phones.

One UI 9.5 Beta is an ‘early look’

There are a couple of reasons the One UI 9.5 beta packs a substantial punch on your Galaxy S26. For one, it’s a halfway mark between Android versions where more useful features can be implemented. Samsung started this trend of releasing the next half-step up in One UI versions with its standard flagships. That’s why, when the Galaxy S27 becomes official, it will launch with One UI 9.5 preloaded.

Samsung details some of the key changes we’ll see in the One UI 9.5 beta, like a new journaling app and better video/camera controls.

Enhanced Pro and Pro Video

	

Mindful note

Medications

Reminders and tracking

Floating shortcuts

Keep essential controls within reach

Improved hearing aid controls

App Lock

Secures individual apps for safer everyday use

Which devices get One UI 9.5 Beta?

It might be because the Galaxy S27 is the first device slated for the stable One UI 9.5 launch, but the Galaxy S26, Galaxy S26 Plus, and Galaxy S26 Ultra are the only devices that can access the beta update. The list doesn’t include the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Fold 8 Ultra, even though they’ve become some of the best devices Samsung has to offer.

Samsung also puts limitations on regions, noting the program will only be open in Germany, India, Korea, Poland, the UK, and the US. Users on other devices outside of those regions won’t be able to download the beta.

That isn’t to say they’re locked out forever. Samsung will very likely expand the beta program before the Galaxy S27 launch, meaning more devices will get access and in wider areas.

How to install the One UI 9.5 beta update

On your Galaxy S26, S26 Plus, or S26 Ultra, you’ll need to sign up for the One UI beta program once more. This is an entirely new beta program, and it doesn’t look like participants carry over from the One UI 9 beta.

Head over to the Samsung Members app on your Galaxy phone.

Scroll down and tap the card in the Beta program section.

Tap One UI 9.5 Beta and hit Join.

Tap again and hit Check for software update.

Alternatively, check your settings.

Update if available.

Once you finish that process, you should be all set with One UI 9.5 beta.

Once again, since it’s early access, you shouldn’t expect things to be perfect. If you find the experience is awful, you can always revert back.

The full One UI 9.5 Beta changelog

Samsung published the full changelog alongside its OTA update, as outlined below.

One UI 9.5 Beta

Camera

Improved camera controls and zoom bar

Quick controls are now laid out on one screen, so every option is visible without scrolling. The layout of the bottom shutter area has also been improved, providing a cleaner and simpler look.

Enhanced Pro and Pro video modes

You can now create custom buttons and presets, see lens and zoom levels as focal length, fine-tune manual sliders, and monitor your shot with an improved histogram and audio meter.

Lock screen personalization

Live effect for wallpapers

Add depth to your Lock screen wallpaper. As you tilt your device, elements in the image shift at different depths.

More customizable Lock screen clock

You can choose how long the clock with seconds appears on your Lock screen. Choose a timeout of 10 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute, 2 minutes, 5 minutes, or 10 minutes from the settings in the upper-right corner.

Sports animations in Now bar

Animation effects are now available for more sports. Celebrate your favorite team’s goals and victories with special visual effects. You can download these effects in Now bar settings.

Digital Wellbeing

Pause before app launch

Turn on Pause before app launch to add a 10-second pause before a selected app or app category opens. The pause helps you reconsider whether you really need to use the app.

Privacy and security

App lock

Lock individual apps to keep them private. Locked apps require biometrics or your screen lock (PIN, pattern, or password) to open, and their widgets and notification content are hidden, even when someone has access to your unlocked phone.

Privacy display for secure app features (Ultra model only)

Privacy display can now turn on automatically for secure features, including Locked apps, Secret mode in Samsung Browser, private albums in Gallery, and locked notes in Samsung Notes. It also protects notifications panel and Recents previews from any app set to turn on Privacy display automatically.

Fingerprint and face recognition at the same time

Fingerprint and face recognition now work at the same time if you’ve registered both and the feature you’re using supports both verification types. You no longer need an extra tap to use face verification. Just look at the screen or touch the fingerprint sensor to verify your identity.

Redesigned biometric registration

Fingerprint and face registration screens have been redesigned with a cleaner, more refined look.

My Files

Improved document support

You can now open PPTX and DOCX files directly in My Files without installing Microsoft Office or other apps. Document Reader already supports PDF and TXT files.

Easier storage cleanup

When you manage storage in My Files, you now have the option to delete uncategorized and files that are in use in the Other category.

Samsung DeX

Optimized window maximizing

Maximizing a window now fills the entire screen, window controls are now integrated with the status bar at the top of the screen, and the apps background color is visible behind the taskbar at the bottom, providing a more immersive experience.

Auto split and more snap options

You can now snap windows to all four corners in addition to the top, bottom, left, and right. You can also arrange your running apps into 2, 3, or 4 split-screen windows at once.

Samsung Health

Enhanced sleep coaching

You can now start sleep coaching with just 3 days of data from the past two weeks. Check your overall sleep status and get personalized coaching tailored to your sleep patterns and goals.

Scan meals and log them instantly

Take a single photo of a meal before you eat it and get nutrition details, ingredients, and calorie estimates right away. No need to search for and enter every food you ate.

Mindful notes

Clear your mind and record your thoughts with free writing and guided prompts. Your notes sync seamlessly with Mood check-in to reveal your mood trends at a glance.

Track your medications worldwide

The Medications tracker is now available globally. You can enter your medications, set personalized reminders, and track your daily intake all in one place.

Reorder cards

You can now change the order of cards in the Activity, Sleep, Vitals, Mindfulness, and Nutrition tabs. Just drag and drop the cards you use the most to make them easier to find.

Accessibility

Intuitive floating accessibility shortcuts

Access your accessibility features from a floating button that’s always available, without the need to select additional options. Visual on and off indicators make it easy to see which features are available.

Improved hearing aid controls

Adjust your connected hearing aids’ volume from the notification panel. You can also choose which sounds from your phone reach your ears by opting out of notifications or ringtones and alarms.

Even more improvements

Search for Quick panel controls

When editing the Quick panel, you can search by app name or control name to find the controls you want quickly without scrolling through the full list.

Downloadable ringtones

Download past versions of Over the Horizon, Samsung’s signature sound, along with a curated selection of ringtones from past and present Samsung devices. Set any of them as your ringtone or use them for alarms.

Other changes

Audio brief and Moments no longer available

Audio brief and Moments will no longer be available in Now brief after you upgrade to One UI 9.5.

One UI 9.5 beta is available now for the Galaxy S26 series.

title: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign sounds like exactly what I’ve been wanting
snippet: Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models. more…
fullText:
Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models.

Weighing the pros and cons of Apple’s expanding iPhone lineup

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include new models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”

That problem isn’t going away, since the iPhone Duo represents a brand new type of iPhone that some users will love, while others find it isn’t for them.

With my failed iPhone Duo experiment over, I’m back to using iPhone 18 Pro as my default model. But I still have an iPhone Air around for work, and every time I pick it up, I’m struck by how impressive it remains.

I used the iPhone Air all of last year and loved it. The main reason I upgraded to an iPhone 18 Pro is the camera system. I have young children at home—including newborn twins—and want to capture the best possible photos before they get older. 

iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera has been fantastic, and it’s great having the Telephoto again too.

But I still sorely miss the overall design of the iPhone Air. And it sounds like next year, I could get the best of both models.

‘iPhone 20 Pro’ could combine the best of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Air design

Rumors indicate Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models will have a unique new design featuring a quad-curved display that makes it look bezel-free.

The new models are expected to also be a bit slimmer, use curved edges, and possibly even bring back titanium. Leakers say the new design borrows a lot from the iPhone Air’s look.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

While the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ certainly won’t—and shouldn’t—be as thin as iPhone Air, if it can slim down a little and adopt several other Air design traits, I suspect it will evoke the same affection the Air has.

But unlike the Air, the new Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

title: Samsung’s Galaxy S27 redesign is ‘100%’ confirmed, leaker says – do you like it? [Poll]
snippet: Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it? more…
fullText:
Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it?

To say that Galaxy smartphone design has been stale is a bit of an understatement. The same core design has been in use for over half a decade at this point, with only the smallest tweaks in the past few generations. And it’s been a problem, too. While Samsung insists that the vertical triple camera array is the company’s “core identity,” it also means that the industry’s move to magnetic wireless charging and accessories are essentially incompatible with Galaxy devices.

Related: Samsung says Galaxy S26 vertical camera is a ‘core identity’ — it’s also a core problem

Finally, changes are incoming.

We’ve seen repeated leaks of the Galaxy S27 series so far with a new full-width camera island on the Ultra and Pro models, and leaker Ice Universe says that this design is now “100%” confirmed, with the final design having two larger camera lenses on the left side, a smaller lens on the bottom right, and a flash above that. We saw this same design in a leak earlier this month, which Ice said at the time was “wrong,” presumably because the flash was replaced by a fourth camera in the dummy unit. 

	

But the question at this point is, do you even like this new look?

Personally, I’m on the fence. I’m thrilled Samsung is finally doing away with the table-rocking, Qi2-ruining vertical array, but I’m not exactly happy we’re getting an iPhone clone as a result. I’d say beggars can’t be choosers, but this is Samsung we’re talking about – I think it’s fair to ask for a bit more.

What do you think?

title: iOS 27 has clever new Messages feature I’ve been using a lot
snippet: iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

Messages adds Smart Reply feature that’s personalized to you in iOS 27

When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were announced in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

The idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18. 

Fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:

Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

Before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

The only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

title: iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration
snippet: iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below. more…
fullText:
iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

iFixit tears Apple HomeView apart in more ways than one

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

	

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

title: Apple Calendar got two feature upgrades it really needed in iOS 27
snippet: Apple Calendar keeps getting better, including some design updates coming in iOS 27.3. But there are two standout feature upgrades added recently in iOS 27 that Apple’s Calendar app really needed. more…
fullText:
Apple Calendar keeps getting better, including some design updates coming in iOS 27.3. But there are two standout feature upgrades added recently in iOS 27 that Apple’s Calendar app really needed.

#1: Natural language input for events

I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it. But one key area the app has long lagged behind competitors is event creation.

When you need to create a new event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc. By contrast, the excellent third-party app Fantastical lets you type in natural language and it automatically fills in relevant parameters based on what you type.

In iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events. You can type out your event details and certain recognized parameters will be used to automatically fill in the detail fields. 

While the feature still isn’t on par with what Fantastical offers, since it doesn’t support as many data points as the third-party alternative, it’s very much a step in the right direction.

#2: Using Siri AI to create multiple events at once, edit events, and more

Apple has always pitched Siri as being like a personal assistant. As such, calendar-related tasks should have been Siri’s strong suit. But until iOS 27, you couldn’t actually manage your calendar very well using Siri.

With Siri AI, that’s changed in a big way. Now, you can do things like:

have Siri add a bunch of events to your Calendar at once, for example your kid’s sports schedule or school holidays

make edits to existing events using natural language, for example “Move today’s lunch to next Wednesday instead”

ask detailed questions about upcoming events naturally, without needing to use precise syntax for Siri to find them

One of my favorite personal examples is from this summer when the NFL schedule was released. I asked Siri to find the Dallas Cowboys schedule and add every game to my calendar, and it pulled this off with ease.

Siri is so much better than before at assisting with your calendar, and iOS 27.3 will bring even more capabilities soon.

title: Microsoft is shutting down the ‘To Do’ app that replaced Wunderlist, with no real replacement
snippet: Microsoft announced this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it. more…
fullText:
Microsoft announced this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The company explains:

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the new private plan. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020. 

Microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business users. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

title: YouTube Music removing Samples tab on Android & iOS
snippet: YouTube Music is simplifying its core navigation on Android and iOS by removing the Samples tab, though the vertical video format remains in the app. more…
fullText:
YouTube Music is simplifying its core navigation on Android and iOS by removing the Samples tab, though the vertical video format remains in the app.

The bottom bar is now just Home, Search, and Library for Premium subscribers. YouTube introduced the Samples feed in 2023 as a way to discover new songs via a Shorts-esque format. Tapping the tab opened a video player that cycled through the “latest release from an up-and-coming artist or a deep cut from a legacy artist” you might like.

	

While it’s no longer accessible from the navigation bar, Samples remains available on playlist, artist, and album pages in the top-right corner for a more focused experience.

This server-side change has been slowly rolling out in recent weeks, and we’re now seeing wider availability. For free users, “Upgrade” remains as a fourth tab. 

	

Meanwhile, YouTube Music has rolled out visual tweaks to buttons on the album and playlist pages. Play is now on the right, while download, add to library, and comments are grouped together at the left.

Looking ahead, YouTube announced in September that Ask Music will soon be accessible from the top-right corner. This Gemini spark icon is slowly rolling out to users.

Whether you’re paying closer attention to family health or simply want better-tasting water for coffee and cooking, Waterdrop Filter has options for different kitchens and budgets. From a Waterdrop reverse osmosis system for a busy family kitchen to a countertop dispenser for a smaller apartment, here’s how to find a home water upgrade that fits your routine.

Under-sink RO systems for busy family kitchens

The best under-sink water filter for your home depends in part on how many people are filling glasses and cooking at once. For families of six or more and frequent hosts, the Waterdrop X16 Alkaline Mineral Reverse Osmosis System is the flagship option.

Its capacity of up to 1,600 gallons per day helps keep water flowing when everyone’s getting ready in the morning or preparing a holiday meal. The 11-stage filtration system adds calcium and magnesium back after reverse osmosis for a more balanced taste, while the tankless design leaves more room beneath the sink.

The smart faucet lets you check filter life at a glance. The X16 is known for its fast dispensing and compact design. During the sale, it’s $1,299, down from $1,999, saving $700, or ~35%.

For a family of four or five, the Waterdrop G3P800 Reverse Osmosis System brings under-sink reverse osmosis to the kitchen for less. It offers up to 800 gallons per day, with 10-stage filtration, UV sterilization, and a smart faucet that shows filter status.

Both systems have a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio, producing three parts filtered water for each part sent to the drain. Waterdrop says the X16 and G3P800 help reduce contaminants including lead, PFOA, and PFOS. Waterdrop also lists NSF/ANSI certifications for both models, covering reverse osmosis performance and lead content in the materials. The G3P800 carries additional certifications covering taste-related filtration and specific contaminant-reduction claims.

G3P800 is recognized for its straightforward filter changes and the difference it makes for water, coffee, and tea. It’s $699 during the sale, down from $999, for $300 in savings and 30% off.

Hot and cold water right from your countertop

If you’re shopping for a reverse osmosis water filter, countertop models make it possible to upgrade without changing the plumbing beneath your sink. Renters, apartment residents, and anyone who wants water ready for tea at the touch of a button may prefer a countertop RO system.

The Waterdrop M6CG Mineral Hot & Cold Reverse Osmosis System combines countertop reverse osmosis, remineralization, and hot and cold dispensing in one appliance. Its 59°F to 203°F temperature range covers everything from a cool glass of water to tea, cocoa, and other hot drinks.

Five volume settings and a customizable Favorite Mode let you save your preferred temperature and serving size. There’s also a detachable 40-ounce glass pitcher you can carry straight to the dinner table, which is handy for family meals and holiday hosting. Separate feed-water and wastewater tanks keep the two apart, and the M6CG has the same 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio as the under-sink models.

The M6CG is $409 during the sale, down from $539, saving $130, or ~24%.

For a more affordable countertop water filtration system, the Waterdrop CT01 Instant Hot & Cold Water Filter Dispenser offers the same temperature range with six-stage non-RO filtration. It helps reduce chlorine, rust, and sediment while retaining minerals, and it produces no wastewater.

Like the M6CG, the CT01 requires no installation. Its 1.32-gallon tank means fewer trips to refill it throughout the day, whether you’re keeping water on hand at your desk or making another round of tea. For winter hydration, having hot and cold filtered water ready in one place is a convenient addition to the kitchen.

The CT01 is $199.99 during the Black Friday sale (20% off).

A simple water filter for about $90

If you mainly want to improve the taste of the water from your existing tap, the Waterdrop TSA 8 Layer Under Sink Water Filter System is an accessible place to start.

It connects to your cold-water line and uses eight-stage filtration to help reduce chlorine, sediment, and other impurities. Replacement schedules vary by cartridge, from about six months for the pre-filter to as long as 18 months for the carbon block filter, depending on usage and water quality.

The TSA is $90.24, down from $119.99, saving $29.75, or approximately 25%.

title: Google confirms huge list of new Home features, including three Nest Thermostat upgrades
snippet: Google Home is constantly rolling out new updates and, today, the company is detailing some of its latest updates including a faster Gemini for Home experience and an upcoming Nest Thermostat upgrade. more…
fullText:
Google Home is constantly rolling out new updates and, today, the company is detailing some of its latest updates including a faster Gemini for Home experience and an upcoming Nest Thermostat upgrade.

In a post today, Google details several Google Home updates that are widely rolling out to users.

The first was announced last week – home keys in Google Wallet. This leverages compatible NFC and UWB (Aliro) locks on newer Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy smartphones, letting you unlock your door by simply tapping your phone. 

Google also says that Google Home Premium Advanced subscribers should see audio descriptions accompanying event descriptions from camera and doorbell events, including breaking glass or barking dogs. This adds more context to these already-useful alerts.

	

Cameras are also getting an upgrade for Activity Zones:

…we’ve tightened Activity Zone boundary precision on our newest wired cameras to significantly reduce false alerts from passing cars, animals, and motion just outside your zone borders. We also redesigned the camera settings page to put Activity Zones front and center, and added a confirmation prompt on iOS when exiting an edited zone so you never accidentally lose your custom boundaries.

The Google Home website also gets faster scrubbing and new keyboard shortcuts – Left or Right arrow keys skip back or forward in 5-second increments, rapidly to jump 30 seconds or more.

Gemini for Home continues to get faster, with Google saying that the latest updates have resulted in an overall speed improvement of 20% on “everyday requests.” Gemini for Home has also expanded to six new countries including India, Taiwan, Singapore, Colombia, South Korea, and Brazil starting “next month.”

Finally, Google is also preparing some useful upgrades for Nest Thermostat.

The first is a dashboard for Nest Thermostat users in the US and Canada that shows “estimated cumulative savings” spurred by their thermostat. You’ll be able to see these savings in “the Climate space, thermostat controller, and Favorites widget.” The second is the abiltiy to use third-party room temperature sensors with the 4th-Gen Nest Learning Thermostat. Google has its own sensor for this that sells for $40, but there are more affordable alternatives that often bring more functionality too, so this is a really nice addition. Compatible brands will include IKEA, Eve, and Aqara.

Google explains:

Starting in December, Nest thermostat owners in the U.S. and Canada can check the app to see estimated cumulative savings. And they can also balance hot and cold spots with compatible third-party room sensors with their 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat.

A third update is to the Dynamic Farsight faces on the latest Nest Learning Thermostat. “New” faces are coming with “designs to match your aesthetics,” while a new Lunar face will track moon phases.

Dynamic Farsight already lets you see the time, temperature, weather, and air quality from across the room, and starting this December, we’re rolling out new Dynamic Farsight faces with designs that match your aesthetics. Keep an eye out for seasonal animations on the Temperature face, or switch to our new Lunar face to track the phases of the moon right on your wall.
